2:2.t: "The day of Christ": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "the day of the Lord". "Is at hand": the KJV's reading; the Greek enesteken usually means "has come" or "is already here".

2:3.t: "The man of sin": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "the man of lawlessness". "Doomed to destruction": the KJV's "the son of perdition"; see John 17:12.
"The rebellion" (Greek apostasia): the KJV's "a falling away", a revolt against God.

2:8.t: "The Lord": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "the Lord Jesus". Echoes Isaiah 11:4.

2:13.t: "From the beginning": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts read "as firstfruits".

3:3.t: "The evil one": the KJV's "evil"; the Greek can mean either.

1:9.t: "Everlasting destruction" (Greek olethron aionion): ruin of the age to come, separation "from the presence of the Lord". Christians differ on whether this means conscious, unending punishment or final destruction; the Bible's language includes both pictures.

2:6.t: "What is holding him back ... the one who now holds it back" (Greek to katechon ... ho katechon): neuter, then masculine. Paul had told the Thessalonians what he meant (2:5), but we do not know. Suggestions include the Roman Empire and its ruler, the rule of law, the preaching of the gospel, or the Holy Spirit.

2:7.t: "The secret power of lawlessness" (Greek to mysterion tes anomias): the KJV's "the mystery of iniquity". "Holds it back": the KJV's "letteth", which in 1611 meant "hinders".

2:15.t: "Teachings" (Greek paradoseis): the KJV's "traditions", what was handed down by the apostles, whether by word or letter.

3:6.t: "Idle and disruptive" (Greek ataktos): the KJV's "disorderly", originally a soldier out of rank. Some had stopped working, perhaps expecting the Lord's immediate return.
